questions.q: What are the two protagonists' names in "Lost Spring," and which story does each belong to?
questions.a: The two protagonists are Saheb (from "Sometimes I find a Rupee in the garbage") and Mukesh (from "I want to drive a car"). A wrong answer — such as naming only one protagonist or confusing their stories — reveals the student has not grasped the dual-narrative structure of the chapter, which is essential because CBSE questions often ask for comparative analysis across both stories.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Saheb's name "Saheb-e-Alam" (lord of the universe) is ironic, using one specific detail from the text.
questions.a: The name means "lord of the universe," but Saheb is a barefoot ragpicker who scrounges in garbage dumps and later becomes a tea-stall worker with no autonomy — the steel canister "belongs to the man who owns the tea shop." A wrong answer that only defines the name without contrasting it with his reality shows the student understands the literal meaning but misses the literary device of irony, which CBSE explicitly tests in "Thinking about language" questions.

questions.q: The text says: "The steel canister seems heavier than the plastic bag he would carry so lightly over his shoulder." Apply the concept of symbolism to explain what the canister and the bag each represent for Saheb.
questions.a: The plastic bag represents Saheb's freedom and ownership — "The bag was his" — while the steel canister represents his loss of agency — "The canister belongs to the man who owns the tea shop. Saheb is no longer his own master!" A wrong answer that describes only the physical weight difference misses the symbolic layer; CBSE marking schemes award marks for linking objects to abstract ideas like freedom vs. bondage.

questions.q: Compare how Saheb and Mukesh each respond to their circumstances. Analyze whether their responses are shaped more by individual agency or by structural forces (caste, poverty, law).
questions.a: Saheb internalizes helplessness — he accepts the tea-stall job, loses his "carefree look," and the text notes "promises like mine abound in every corner of his bleak world." Mukesh asserts agency — "I will be a motor mechanic," "I will walk" to the garage — but his dream hits a structural ceiling: "Few airplanes fly over Firozabad." Both are shaped overwhelmingly by structural forces (Saheb by migration and statelessness; Mukesh by caste-bound bangle-making and police-middlemen nexus), but Mukesh's fleeting defiance makes the tragedy sharper. A wrong answer that calls both "poor children" without differentiating their psychological responses fails the analytical depth required for 6-mark questions.

questions.q: Evaluate the author's choice to end Mukesh's story with his silence about flying planes ("He is suddenly silent. 'No,' he says, staring at the ground."). Is this an effective character moment? Justify with two reasons.
questions.a: Yes, it is effective. First, the silence contrasts with his earlier direct eye contact and verbal certainty ("I will learn to drive a car"), showing how structural limits (no planes over Firozabad, no pathway beyond mechanic) silently crush aspiration. Second, the phrase "embarrassment that has not yet turned into regret" captures the precise emotional stage of a child realizing his dream has a ceiling — more powerful than explicit anger. A wrong answer that calls it "sad" without analyzing the narrative technique (contrast, understatement, free indirect discourse) misses the literary analysis skill CBSE rewards.

questions.q: Write a 4-line diary entry from Saheb's perspective on his first day at the tea stall, using one metaphor from the text and showing his internal conflict.
questions.a: Sample: "The steel canister is an anchor around my neck — shiny, cold, not mine. I stirred tea for men who laughed loud; my plastic bag waits in the corner, light as a forgotten kite. They paid me 800 rupees. I forgot how to smile." A poor answer writes a generic complaint without the metaphor ("anchor," "kite") or the textual callback (plastic bag vs. canister, 800 rupees), showing the student cannot transfer textual evidence into creative voice — a skill tested in CBSE writing tasks.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the ______ examines the central character's traits, motivations, conflicts, and development across the narrative, using textual evidence to reveal how the author constructs the character to embody the story's core themes.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you're a journalist interviewing Saheb at the tea stall and ______ in the dark hutment — what would their answers reveal about their inner worlds?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can independently write a structured 150-word character analysis for either Saheb or Mukesh using the PEEL method (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link), identifying at least three character traits supported by specific textual details, and explaining how each trait connects to the theme of stolen childhood.
